item.title: Trump fires back at efforts to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday, alleging that the embattled Pentagon chief had committed "high crimes and misdemeanors" and abused the power of his office by violating the War Powers Resolution, conducting military operations without congressional authorization and ordering unlawful military actions in several countries. The expected impeachment filing came as Congress returned to Washington, D.C. , to begin a lame-duck session following the historic rout that the GOP suffered in last week's midterm elections . Hegseth is facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran, which some top Republicans — including Trump — blame in part for the drubbing that cost them control of Congress. "Despite the absence of a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack upon the United States," Massie said in a speech on the House floor, "Secretary Hegseth knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation." Massie said Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law." His actions thus "warrant impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States," the Kentucky Republican said. President Trump on Monday pledged to support Hegseth while he faces impeachment. "Yeah, I'll stand by him," he told CNN , adding that he believes Massie "has a lot of hatred in his heart." Hegseth leaves a meeting of defense ministers in the Philippines on Oct. 28. Pool via Getty Images Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the GOP primary — first introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote. It's unclear whether an impeachment effort will succeed in the House, which is still under Republican control, but Massie told ABC News that he's "confident there will be enough GOP defectors for it to pass." To do so, the resolution requires a simple majority, meaning that just three Republicans would need to vote with all Democrats to prevail. A vote could come as soon as this week. Trump has repeatedly insisted that he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief, at least not yet. "No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters last week. The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor. "I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat. CBS News , however, reported last week that Trump "has been asking advisers" whether he should stay or go. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices. He has also been among the advisers urging Trump to restart the war. He and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, have supported a return to major combat operations against Iran during recent briefings on military options, the Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 6, while Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff have pushed for diplomacy to end the conflict. The U.S. Capitol building is seen in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4. Kevin Carter/Getty Images Trump acknowledged on Nov. 4 that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vance was unequivocal. "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X . "The reason we lost is the war." The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did. Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning." "He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress." Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him. "I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. "He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it." Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said on Nov. 6 that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth." "We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran," Comer told NewsNation . "No one's happy about Iran." A fire burns at an oil depot in Tehran, Iran, on March 8 after U.S. and Israeli attacks. Hassan Ghaedi/Anadolu via Getty Images When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list. "In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker in January, said at a rally last month . Hegseth, for his part, has remained defiant. In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to X on Nov. 5, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke") and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit. "A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me." Hegseth said on Monday that he's "not worried about" the impeachment efforts. The defense secretary said he would address the topic at a press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday. This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/articles-of-impeachment-against-hegseth-introduced-in-the-house-as-gop-criticism-over-the-iran-war-mounts-after-midterm-rout-194929419.html

item.title: Trump's MAHA coalition faces new tensions as former officials trade accusations
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A public spat between former Trump administration officials over alleged corruption in public health policymaking is the latest front in Republicans' postelection recriminations, a battle that has exposed fault lines within the White House and could reshape political alliances involving the influential Make America Healthy Again movement. The blowup began when Calley Means , a former top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a chief advocate for the MAHA movement , appeared on Joe Rogan's podcast Friday and accused Susie Wiles, James Blair and others of catering to foreign and domestic lobbyists at the expense of Americans' health. Wiles, who was recently replaced as White House chief of staff, and Blair, a top political adviser, have denied the allegations. Means' remarks came days after voters cast ballots in midterm elections where government corruption was among the top issues for voters who ousted Republicans and handed Democrats control of Congress. The issue overlaps with concerns from MAHA activists, who have been focused on combating what they see as systemic and harmful corporate influence over policymaking. MAHA became an important part of Trump's coalition after Kennedy endorsed him during the last presidential campaign, and fractures could create political headaches or new avenues for congressional investigations in the coming years. Zen Honeycutt, a former Kennedy campaign staffer and founder of the group Moms Across America, said Means is "amplifying the frustrations that a lot of MAHA folks have had the past few months and validating them." She's "excited for a new beginning" now that Trump has replaced Wiles with Stephen Miller, whom she views as more aligned with the movement. But Honeycutt hasn't ruled out working with Democrats, such as New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whom she met with in July to discuss shared environmental priorities, including the pesticide glyphosate and artificial intelligence data centers. "The MAHA movement does not belong to any party or politician," Honeycutt said. Means alleges outside interests influenced policymaking On Rogan's show, Means recounted a conversation he had with Wiles about her declining to support certain MAHA initiatives because she needed donations from the sugar industry. "Calley, we can't do this. I need sugar money," he recalled Wiles saying to him. "I need the money from the sugar people to win the midterms." "There is a very concentrated group in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for," Means said. Rogan's show was released Friday, shortly before Trump announced Wiles would step down as White House chief of staff. Means was hired as a White House adviser early in the second Trump administration. He used his perch at the Health and Human Services Department to attack the nation's leading physician groups, federal agencies and government scientists , claiming they only protect their own interests . Means left the Trump administration in October, without stating a reason for his exit. "She has taken a stranglehold on any policy decision" impacting the MAHA movement, alongside her former lobbying firm Ballard Partners, Means said about Wiles. Referring to Blair in the Rogan interview, Means said he has "explicitly catered to special interests against the will of the voters." He said he believed much of what he was alleging "happened without Trump's full knowledge." Blair, who previously served as a White House deputy chief of staff before taking an outside role in Trump's political operation, responded on social media that he was contemplating suing Means over his statements. In text messages between Means and Blair, viewed by The Associated Press, Blair told Means "if you get near slandering or defaming me I will sue you," and "if you are gonna try to knife me, I'm happy to return the favor." The White House denied Means' accusations. "The Trump Administration has never allowed and will never allow outside groups to influence policy decisions," White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said. Brian Ballard, founder of Ballard Partners, denied communicating with top White House officials on glyphosate and other issues in a statement posted on social media. MAHA support may be up for grabs The extraordinary public fight, which was continuing on social media Monday, comes after MAHA had grown disenchanted over some of the administration's moves. In recent months, many grassroots MAHA activists who had initially hoped to collaborate with Trump's Environmental Protection Agency had soured on the agency and the administration, viewing them as infiltrated by lobbyist interests. They pointed to various insiders in the agricultural and chemical industries who'd secured high-level positions in the EPA and blamed them for the administration's failure to pass meaningful reforms to address microplastics in drinking water or pesticides on farms. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin promised last December to unveil a formal agenda of MAHA policies he would act on. But by the summer, the so-called MAHA agenda had never surfaced, and an EPA spokesperson told the AP that MAHA is an ongoing effort, rather than a single report. That apparent reversal prompted several activists to say they planned to vote on issues over party in November's elections. "People are done with the profits of corporations being prioritized over public health," Alexandra Muñoz, a molecular toxicologist who collaborates with MAHA activists on certain issues, told the AP in July. "And I think that will have an important role in the midterms." The simmering MAHA frustration, coupled with Means' allegations, could put MAHA support in play for Democrats, something Means himself suggested over the weekend. "There's a lot of complicated issues that I'm sure Democrats are going to want to address. But when it comes to these issues on MAHA, I think there is huge opportunity in the next year to get some big things done," he told CBS' "Face the Nation." But doing so poses its own complications. Democrats who will take over both chambers of Congress next year could use Means' statements as a vehicle to begin investigations into White House officials. Some Democrats have long sought to investigate Kennedy over his upending of vaccine policy and his vast cuts to science research, among other decisions. Pushing hard against Kennedy, however, could complicate efforts to build closer ties with MAHA supporters, many of whom still view the health secretary positively. Means' interviews included a profuse defense of Kennedy, who some have speculated could attempt another run for president in 2028. Means called Kennedy a "hero" on the podcast interview. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/feud-between-former-trump-officials-205942168.html

item.title: FBI investigating Nvidia CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy, Trump says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Steve Holland, Courtney Rozen, Karen Freifeld and David Shepardson WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Monday the FBI was looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. Trump said he "was amazed" by allegations about Huang, ‌among the president's closest allies in Silicon Valley. Trump said he had spoken to the CEO, who told him that he had no idea that ‌the woman was a spy. "I know the FBI is looking into it," Trump said. "I think that he'll be in good shape," he added. Nvidia shares closed down more than 4% on Monday after the company's board launched ​an internal investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The probe, announced on Sunday, has put a spotlight on 63-year-old Huang's future given Nvidia's status as the world's most valuable chipmaker and the CEO's role as the most prolific salesman of the AI boom. Huang told Nvidia's employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship. The leather-jacketed Huang enjoys rock-star status worldwide, particularly in Asia, where he often mingles freely with fans, taking selfies and signing autographs for his devoted followers. He ‌is Nvidia's fifth-largest shareholder with a roughly 3.6% stake, according ⁠to LSEG data, and keeps a tight grip on the company through an unusually flat structure in which dozens of executives report directly to him. But unlike Mark Zuckerberg's Meta Platforms or Elon Musk's SpaceX, Nvidia has no dual-class shares that would give co-founder Huang majority ⁠voting control. The New York Times reported that Trump was briefed on Huang's relationship with the woman and that she was giving information to the Chinese government, and that the president chose not to act on the information. "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing. Huang's relationship with Trump ​has ​coincided with several favorable policy developments for the company, and the president has lavished Huang with praise, ​awarding him the nation's highest honor for scientific achievement in October. The ‌same day Trump gave Huang the award, the president disclosed buying up to $1.6 million and selling up to $1 million of Nvidia shares during the summer. 'NOT AN ORDINARY CEO' Nvidia said its board has confidence in Huang, thought by many on Wall Street to be the most important person underpinning the AI trade. Analysts acknowledged uncertainty around succession, but most do not expect the investigation to result in the longtime CEO stepping down. "Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he is Nvidia, clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction, and pulls most of the company's strings himself," said Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein. Nvidia shareholders were quick to sue Huang and the ‌company in a proposed class action on Monday, accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang's ​ties with a suspected Chinese spy. Lawmakers and advocates told Reuters that Congress was more likely to pass ​legislation to tighten China's access to AI chips in light of news of ​Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence agent. US House of Representatives Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday that Congress needs more answers ‌and called for the House to pass an annual defense bill ​that includes restrictions on chip sales to China. The ​New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed did not respond immediately to a request for comment on Monday, a public holiday in Singapore. Alice Huang did not ​respond to the New York Times last month when it ‌first reported her relationship with Huang, and Reuters could not determine her location to seek comment on Monday. (Additional reporting by Kyu-seok Shim and Heekyong Yang ​in Seoul, Tom Westbrook in Sydney, Roger Tung and Ben Blanchard in Taipei, Danilo Masoni in Milan and Aditya Soni in Bengaluru; Writing by ​Brenda Goh and Sayantani Ghosh; Editing by Ed Davies, Jamie Freed and Arun Koyyur) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.finance.yahoo.com/news/south-korea-says-nvidia-issues-022650481.html

item.title: In a nail-biter Senate race, incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith stays out of view in Mississippi
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom, left, and GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, right. - Rogelio V. Solis/Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc./Getty Images As the Mississippi Senate race still remains too close to call, Democrat Scott Colom and GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith have taken completely different approaches towards the public. Since Election Day, Colom has held at least eight events and capitalized on the national attention of the race to flood the airwaves and make his case for why Democrats should no longer count out a state historically considered a Republican stronghold. Meanwhile, Hyde-Smith has not been seen publicly since she left her election night watch party just outside of Jackson after declaring that she would remain her state’s junior senator. While Colom has appeared at local universities, a Black-owned bookshop, a vinyl record store, a diner, and a senior citizens center and sat for multiple interviews with the media, Hyde-Smith has made her statements solely on X, including posting a Bible verse about hope on Sunday. “Ultimately, at some point, the senator needs to speak out. Where is Cindy Hyde-Smith?” Colom told reporters on Friday at the senior citizens facility in Jackson. “We want to hear from her. She needs to answer questions. What is her path to victory? She doesn’t have one.” Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager Jake Monssen said in a statement to CNN, “Senator Hyde-Smith and our team are working around the clock across Mississippi to protect the integrity of this election and to ensure every legal vote is counted.” As the Senate returned to session on Monday after a six-week recess, Hyde-Smith repeatedly declined to answer questions from reporters in the Capitol hallways about her election. “We’re still counting votes,” she eventually said as reporters trailed her through the building. Hyde-Smith did not answer when asked if she’ll go to court for a recount if she ultimately loses. Asked if she was surprised by the results of the race, the senator said she was surprised by the reporters following her. The divergent strategies speak to a dynamic that played out across the country this election cycle where Republicans in GOP strongholds like Hyde-Smith, who did not work to get ahead of the worsening national political landscape, were caught flatfooted and now find themselves in a once-unthinkable position. Now, Colom leads the incumbent senator by 2,500 votes in a race that could come down to thousands of provisional ballots, which election officials will vet in the coming days. If he wins, he will be Mississippi’s first Democratic senator in nearly four decades and its first Black senator since the Reconstruction era. Hyde-Smith’s campaign refused Colom’s invitations to debate prior to Election Day and did relatively few campaign events even as Colom was frequently on the trail and appearing with top Democrats like Kamala Harris and Bill Clinton. Even some of Hyde-Smith’s supporters have noticed their senator’s absence and how Colom has filled that void. A sign supporting Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith at a gas station in Brandon, Mississippi, on November 8, 2026. - Ellen Schmidt/AP John, an insurance adjuster from Hyde-Smith’s hometown of Brookhaven who declined to disclose his last name, is disappointed the Republican senator did not win in a landslide. Describing his community as the buckle to the Bible Belt, a county where Hyde-Smith outperformed Colom nearly 2:1, it’s hard for him to picture his home state turning blue. But John said he wished Hyde-Smith matched the television ads that he was inundated by from the Colom campaign. “I would like to personally have seen more campaigning from Cindy,” he told CNN. “I would like to have seen more ads for Cindy and put her name out there a little more. And it may be because she’s an incumbent and maybe didn’t feel like the need was there. I’m not sure. I don’t know.” For F.B. Warren, who has served on school boards with Hyde-Smith, Colom’s campaign should be a wakeup call for Republicans about how to not take Mississippi for granted. “It’s kind of like the team that plays a game of football, baseball, basketball, and they never have competition,” Warren told CNN. “So, in Mississippi and across the country, from the Republican Party standpoint, they got pushed. They now got pushed, so they’re going to have to get better. They’re going to have to campaign better. They’re going to have to have better candidates. They’re going to have to work harder, and that’s the big wake-up call.” His wife, Angie Warren, who owns two small stores in Hyde-Smith’s hometown, reflected on how Democrats did more to capitalize on voter enthusiasm this election season. “I do think that the Democratic Party has a better turnout for elections than the Republican Party. I don’t know why that is. I don’t know if they speak closer to the people and they get out and vote more. But for some reason, the Republican Party doesn’t always have the voter turnout that it needs,” she told CNN. While Mississippi has long been Republican territory, Colom and other Democrats have argued that the headwinds against the party in power and the state’s significant Black electorate made the state fertile ground for a flip this cycle. Further, Hyde-Smith, who was first appointed to the Senate in 2018, underperformed Republicans in 2020 as well, winning a full term by 10 points even as Trump won the state by 16. Democratic candidate for Senate Scott Colom speaks to reporters during a campaign event at the Tougaloo Senior Citizens Center in Jackson, Mississippi, on November 6, 2026. - Ellen Schmidt/AP The early lack of national attention to the race gave Colom a long runway to capitalize on Hyde-Smith’s uneven campaign performance. It wasn’t until late October that the Senate Leadership Fund, the leading GOP super PAC focused on Senate races, made an initial reservation of about $160,000 in Mississippi, according to AdImpact data. That reservation was in response to Senate Democrats announcing that they would spend r oughly $1 million on ads for the race. By that time, Colom had started to galvanize the party behind what was once considered a long-shot bid in a state Trump won two years ago by 23 points. Hyde-Smith has posted on social media since Election Day, including a statement on November 6 stating, “we are not backing down. This election is not over” and vowing to “see this through to the very end!” Mississippi GOP Chair Michael Hurst held a press conference last week to tout the 50-plus volunteer attorneys and observers Republicans had sent across the state, with many more are prepared to jump in to help. “Our attorneys and observers will continue to be in different parts of Mississippi – watching as election commissioners review and process these outstanding ballots, ensuring that our elections are followed and that only ballots which have been legally cast are counted,” he said. unknown content item - Even as both sides prepare for a potential legal battle over the results, Democrat Phillip Rollins told CNN that Colom’s nonstop style channeled the frustration that he and others were feeling in the lead up to the election. “People are fed up,” Rollins, who owns the comic book and record shop where Colom recently campaigned, said. “They need to see the change happen during their lifetime and not have to wait.” This story has been updated with additional details. CNN’s Lauren Fox and Manu Raju contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/09/politics/mississippi-senate-hyde-smith-colom-campaign

item.title: Ohio State suspends fraternity after video shows 2 men engulfed in flames
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — A fraternity at Ohio State University has been temporarily suspended while authorities investigate a video that appears to show two panicked men engulfed in flames. A video shared on social media shows a large group of people standing outside, many wearing the school's red and white colors, laughing and shouting while a man sits on the ground with his sweatpants on fire. He then lunges at a second person and tackles him. The second man's clothing also catches fire, and they both roll on the ground removing their clothes as several onlookers intervene. One appears to be holding a small fire extinguisher. University spokesperson Benjamin Johnson said the school has placed Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity on interim suspension while it investigates, and has referred the matter to university and Columbus police. The university did not say how the fraternity is linked to the event, whether the burned men are students or what condition they were in Monday. "The university is aware of this extremely concerning incident, and the individuals in question are receiving medical care," Johnson said in a statement. "Ohio State is committed to a safe and healthy environment and expects students and student organizations to uphold that commitment and the university's values." Columbus Police Sgt. Joe Albert said it appears the matter took place on Saturday. Police did not receive any calls for service at the location, but someone called police Sunday evening reporting that the video was circulating online, he said. Steve Mitchell, CEO of Sigma Alpha Epsilon, said behavior that violates its high standards has no place in its organization and it will take appropriate action to hold those responsible accountable based on the investigation. "We take this matter seriously and are actively investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident while working closely with university officials and local law enforcement," he said in a statement. More than 60,000 students are enrolled at the university. The episode comes as fraternities are back in the national spotlight in the wake of a former Cornell University student's lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024. ___ Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/ohio-state-suspends-fraternity-while-183707961.html

item.title: The James Gunn-Peter Safran era of DC Studios is over after 4 years
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
James Gunn and Peter Safran are out at DC Studios, with Jeremy Latcham taking over (Credit: Getty Images) After four years at DC Studios, James Gunn and Peter Safran will not be leading the company through its next chapter under Skydance ownership as they are handing the reins over to new president and chief creative officer Jeremy Latcham. In a statement, the two executives spoke with pride of their work at the studio and gave Latcham, who worked with Gunn on the “Guardians of the Galaxy” trilogy at Marvel Studios, their blessing. Skydance says that the duo will “return full time to their creative work,” which includes post-production on the “Superman” sequel “Man of Tomorrow” and work on other DC projects. “Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore ‘Superman’ to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with ‘Peacemaker’, ‘Creature Commandos,’ ‘Lanterns’ and ‘Clayface . ‘ We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with,” Gunn and Safran said. “We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in ‘Man of Tomorrow,’” the duo said. Jeremy Latcham DC Studios Latcham was part of the founding core of Marvel Studios under Kevin Feige and worked on global blockbusters like “Iron Man,” “The Avengers,” and Tom Holland’s “Spider-Man” films. Latcham will lead DC’s film, television and animation slate, overseeing the creative pipeline, along with production, talent and strategy. Latcham, who will begin at DC on Dec. 1, will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, co-chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group. “Jeremy brings a deep reverence for DC and its passionate fanbase, recognizing that they are the very foundation of this storied, multigenerational brand,” said Goldberg and Greenstein. “Under his leadership, every film and television show will be ushered from start to finish through the prism of the legions of fans who love and champion it. Jeremy’s track record exemplifies the excellence he will bring to building out DC and the many beloved characters within it.” “DC’s pantheon of characters is among the most iconic in American popular culture. I’ve had the privilege to help bring some of the most celebrated superhero stories to life on the big screen, and I’m excited and honored for the opportunity to now lead DC Studios into its next era. The chance to steward the incredible cast of DC characters to the screen in a way that excites lifelong fans while introducing their timeless stories to the next generation is a massive responsibility that I do not take lightly,” said Latcham. Gunn and Safran have released three theatrical films since taking over DC Studios, starting with “Superman,” which grossed $618 million worldwide amid strong reviews. But the studio’s follow-up, “Supergirl,” fell flat this past summer, earning just $126.4 million globally. The more modestly budgeted “Batman” villain horror film “Clayface” has fared better, grossing $109 million through its first three weekends in theaters. On the TV side, Gunn and Safran developed hit shows like the John Cena-led “Suicide Squad” spinoff “Peacemaker” and the animated show “Creature Commandos,” as well as the recent hit show “Lanterns.” “James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we’re incredibly proud of. We’re grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand,” David Ellison, chairman and CEO, and Ynon Kreiz, co-CEO, of Skydance said in a statement. “Jeremy has been a longtime creative partner to both, and we have complete confidence that James and Peter will ensure a smooth, collaborative transition and continue this work with care. We look forward to working with Jeremy to build the next generation of DC storytelling and to doubling down on our commitment to fans,” Ellison and Kreiz added. The post James Gunn and Peter Safran Out at DC Studios, Jeremy Latcham Named New President and Chief Creative Officer appeared first on TheWrap . item.title: California’s proposed ‘billionaire tax’ fails to pass
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
California voters rejected Proposition 40, the one-time 5% tax on billionaires, the AP reported Monday. Tech leaders outspent backers roughly 10 to 1 to defeat it, and the founders and economists TechCrunch interviewed before the vote were split on whether it would have driven out wealthy residents or just trimmed their fortunes.
